title: General Chemistry II
full_title: General Chemistry II: Equilibrium, Energy and Rates
tagline: Solutions, reaction rates, equilibrium, acids and bases, solubility, free energy, electrochemistry and nuclear chemistry
summary: Why do reactions stop, how fast do they go, and which way do they run? This course introduces solutions and colligative properties, reaction rates and chemical equilibrium with its applications to acids, bases, buffers and solubility, then connects equilibrium to entropy and free energy, electrochemical cells and nuclear processes.
overview: Equilibrium, energy and rate are the three questions every chemical system answers. General Chemistry II is the second year of the first-year curriculum, and it turns the atomic and stoichiometric foundations of the first course into the quantitative science of solutions, equilibria and energy. Almost every chemical phenomenon a first-year student meets — the pH of a buffer, the voltage of a battery, the solubility of a kidney stone, the rate at which food spoils — is an application of one of the nine chapters that follow.

The subject matters far beyond the first year. Aqueous equilibrium governs the chemistry of the oceans, of blood and of the environment; the free-energy change tells an engineer whether a process will run at all; electrochemistry underpins the transport system the world is moving to; nuclear chemistry underpins both medical imaging and a waste problem that will outlast our civilisation. The chapters are also the prerequisite for every later course in the atlas: the thermodynamics and kinetics courses, the titrimetry of analytical chemistry, and the buffered chemistry of living things all begin here.

The course is organised as a spiral rather than a list. The first three chapters build the tools — the behaviour of liquids and solutions, the rate of reaction, and the equilibrium constant — and the next three apply them to the acid–base and solubility equilibria that dominate aqueous chemistry. The last three widen the view to entropy and free energy, to electrochemical cells, and to the nucleus. Each chapter assumes the ones before it, and the whole course assumes General Chemistry I.

What makes the subject hard is not the mathematics — it is algebra with logarithms — but the number of decisions: which equilibrium is operating, which approximation is legitimate, which species is present in excess. The remedy is the same in every chapter: write the balanced equation, write the equilibrium expression, tabulate the concentrations honestly, and check that the answer has the right order of magnitude. Every worked example in these lessons is chosen to exercise exactly that decision.
outcomes: Explain how intermolecular forces determine vapour pressure, boiling point and phase behaviour, and use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
Calculate colligative properties — vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure — for ideal and dilute solutions.
Express reaction rates, determine rate laws and reaction orders from experimental data, and use integrated rate laws, half-lives and the Arrhenius equation.
Write equilibrium-constant expressions (Kc and Kp), convert between them, and use the reaction quotient to predict the direction of a reaction.
Apply Le Chatelier's principle to changes in concentration, pressure and temperature, and solve equilibrium problems by the ICE-table method.
Calculate the pH of strong and weak acids and bases, of salt solutions and of buffers, and analyse titration curves and the choice of indicators.
Use solubility products and complex-formation constants to predict precipitation, dissolution and selective separation.
Connect ΔH, ΔS and ΔG, predict the sign and temperature dependence of spontaneity, and derive the relation between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant.
Balance redox equations, calculate standard cell potentials and apply the Nernst equation, and describe radioactive decay kinetics, binding energy and the uses of radioisotopes.

chapters.title: Liquids, solutions and colligative properties
chapters.summary: Vapour pressure and phase changes, solubility, Raoult’s law, and the effects of solutes on boiling point, freezing point and osmotic pressure.

chapters.title: Reaction rates
chapters.summary: Rates and rate laws, reaction order, integrated rate laws and half-lives, the Arrhenius equation and catalysts.

chapters.title: Chemical equilibrium
chapters.summary: Dynamic equilibrium, the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the reaction quotient, Le Chatelier’s principle and equilibrium calculations.

chapters.title: Acids and bases
chapters.summary: Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis acids and bases, pH, acid and base dissociation constants, weak acids and bases, polyprotic acids and salts.

chapters.title: Buffers and titrations
chapters.summary: Buffer solutions and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, buffer capacity, titration curves and indicators.

chapters.title: Solubility and complex-ion equilibria
chapters.summary: Solubility products, the common-ion effect, selective precipitation and the formation of complex ions.

chapters.title: Entropy, free energy and spontaneity
chapters.summary: The second law, entropy changes, the Gibbs energy and the link between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant.

chapters.title: Redox reactions and electrochemical cells
chapters.summary: Balancing redox equations, galvanic cells, standard electrode potentials, the Nernst equation and electrolysis.

chapters.title: Nuclear chemistry
chapters.summary: Radioactive decay and its kinetics, nuclear binding energy, fission and fusion, and the uses of radioisotopes in dating and medicine.

history.title: Volta builds the pile
history.detail: Alessandro Volta stacks discs of zinc and silver separated by brine-soaked cardboard and produces the first source of continuous electric current, settling the dispute with Galvani and showing that chemical affinity can be converted directly into electricity.

history.title: Faraday's laws of electrolysis
history.detail: Michael Faraday publishes the quantitative laws of electrolysis — the mass of substance liberated at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed — and with them the vocabulary of electrodes, electrolytes, anions and cations.

history.title: Le Chatelier's principle
history.detail: Henri Le Chatelier states the principle that a system in equilibrium responds to a constraint by shifting so as to partly oppose it, turning qualitative equilibrium chemistry into a predictive science.

history.title: Dissociation and osmotic pressure
history.detail: Svante Arrhenius's theory of electrolytic dissociation and Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff's application of the gas laws to dilute solutions appear together in the first volume of the Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, giving solution equilibrium its quantitative form.

history.title: The Arrhenius equation
history.detail: Arrhenius proposes the exponential dependence of the rate constant on temperature, defining the activation energy and turning the empirical science of reaction rates into the science of chemical kinetics.

history.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
history.detail: Henri Becquerel finds that uranium salts fog photographic plates through black paper, revealing an atomic property unrelated to chemical state — the first evidence that the atom has an internal structure and an internal energy.

history.title: The Curies isolate radium
history.detail: Marie and Pierre Curie announce radium, hundreds of times more active than uranium, and show that radioactivity is an atomic property; the work leads to the 1903 Nobel Prize and to the measurement of the enormous energy stored in the nucleus.

history.title: The proton theory of acids and bases
history.detail: Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted and Martin Johannes Lowry, independently, recast acidity as proton donation and define acids and bases as conjugate pairs, while Gilbert Lewis's electron-pair definition appears the same year.

history.title: Fission discovered
history.detail: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann identify barium among the products of neutron-bombarded uranium, and over the winter Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch interpret the result as the splitting of the nucleus — the origin of both nuclear power and the nuclear age.

references.title: Chemical Principles
references.authors: Peter Atkins, Loretta Jones and Ronald Laverman
references.note: The natural text for this course: equilibrium, entropy and electrochemistry treated with mathematical care but at first-year level.

references.title: Chemistry: The Central Science
references.authors: Theodore L. Brown, H. Eugene LeMay, Bruce E. Bursten and Catherine Murphy
references.note: The broadest of the mainstream texts; good worked examples for aqueous equilibrium and acid–base chemistry.

references.title: Chemistry: A Molecular Approach
references.note: Clear on the microscopic picture behind colligative properties and equilibrium; strong end-of-chapter problems.

references.title: Chemistry
references.note: A companion text with many worked buffer and titration examples.

references.title: Chemistry
references.authors: Steven S. Zumdahl, Susan A. Zumdahl and Donald J. DeCoste
references.note: A problem-heavy text; its treatment of stoichiometry and equilibrium algebra is good practice for this course.

references.title: General Chemistry: Principles and Modern Applications
references.authors: Ralph H. Petrucci, F. Geoffrey Herring, Jeffry D. Rait and Maureen Ryan
references.note: Detailed on solubility equilibria and electrochemistry; useful for the harder exercises.

references.title: Physical Chemistry
references.authors: Peter Atkins and Julio de Paula
